purpose: Private editorial intake for weekly AI risk signals. This file is never published directly.

entries.title: Human approval is ineffective unless it is bound to the exact action that executes
entries.summary: The Loopjacking research describes how a human may approve one operation while mutable workflow state allows a materially different operation to execute later.
entries.whyItMatters: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints can appear in a process map without actually constraining the consequential action.
entries.controlImplication: For material agent workflows, bind approved parameters and context to execution through deterministic or tamper-evident controls, then retain evidence of the executed action.

entries.title: Agent loss of control calls for independent scrutiny and defence in depth
entries.summary: Independent analysis of agent boundary failures points to a combination of enabling environment, sufficient capability and misaligned objectives, with lessons from aviation, nuclear power and cybersecurity.
entries.whyItMatters: The operating environment and the independence of the control are as important as the model’s stated objective.
entries.controlImplication: Use layered safeguards, independent evidence sources, incident taxonomy and post-incident learning rather than relying on a single model-based monitor.

entries.title: Proof that an agent remained within its control envelope may become an assurance output
entries.summary: The Proof-of-Control initiative frames auditability as evidence that a particular action remained authorised, rather than a general claim that a governance framework exists.
entries.whyItMatters: Conventional logs and operator attestations may be too weak when agents act at machine speed across systems.
entries.controlImplication: Define a verifiable evidence standard for material agent actions: identity, authorisation, complete action telemetry, integrity of the record and proof of containment where required.

entries.title: Autonomy should be calibrated to impact, reversibility and verifiability
entries.summary: The useful design alternative to binary agent permission is risk-based autonomy, with tighter intervention requirements as actions become harder to reverse or independently verify.
entries.whyItMatters: A valid identity alone cannot show that an agent’s behaviour is safe once it is inside the perimeter.
entries.controlImplication: Set action tiers using business impact, reversibility and independent verifiability; link each tier to permissions, runtime policy enforcement and human-intervention requirements.

entries.title: A minimum agent control plane is converging around inventory, authority, activity and response
entries.summary: Cross-vendor architecture work centres four operational questions: where agents are, what they can do, what they are doing, and how quickly the firm can respond.
entries.whyItMatters: Those questions create a practical minimum standard across agent inventory, identity, delegated authority, observability and containment.
entries.controlImplication: Require every material agent to be a first-class identity with task-scoped access, traceable delegation, runtime monitoring and rapid reversible containment.

entries.title: UK AI survey exposes the gap between policy adoption and post-deployment controls
entries.summary: The Bank of England and FCA’s 2026 survey covers 196 firms. Among full-survey respondents, 94% reported firm-wide AI policies; ongoing monitoring, leakage testing and periodic review or recertification were each reported by around half. Eighty per cent reported deploying AI agents and 2% reported broad autonomy.
entries.whyItMatters: Reported governance structures are more common than operational evidence after deployment, while the survey is descriptive and is not a control-effectiveness test.
entries.controlImplication: For material AI workflows, test current monitoring coverage, leakage controls and review or recertification, retaining sample evidence, exceptions and resulting changes.

entries.title: LiteLLM compromise turns package installation into a credential exposure test
entries.summary: Microsoft describes the compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release distributed on 21 October. Malicious Python startup files could execute when Python started in affected environments, even without an application importing LiteLLM.
entries.whyItMatters: Exposure may extend from gateways to developer workstations, build agents, test systems and containers; removing only the package may leave startup components or exposed credentials unaddressed.
entries.controlImplication: Identify affected package versions and Python environments without running Python or pip inside a suspect environment; investigate execution evidence and rotate credentials available to affected identities.

sources.title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks

entries.title: OpenAI describes hardened controls for its frontier-model training environment
entries.summary: OpenAI reports that it paused some training and evaluation, hardened infrastructure and monitoring, and now considers no live internet access the responsible approach for frontier training under its present assessment.
entries.whyItMatters: The described controls are the provider’s account of its own environment, not independent evidence that comparable safeguards work across other deployments.
entries.controlImplication: For material AI environments, test network isolation, execution boundaries and intervention controls against documented threat scenarios, and distinguish vendor attestations from independent assurance.

sources.title: Securing our frontier model training environment

entries.title: Anthropic’s S-1 makes frontier-lab economics and dependencies more visible
entries.summary: Anthropic filed an S-1 with the SEC on 26 October and applied to list Class A common stock on Nasdaq under ANT. The public filing leaves offering size and price undecided and describes substantial infrastructure and partner dependencies.
entries.whyItMatters: The filing provides primary financial disclosures for assessing compute commitments, concentration and capital needs, but it does not establish a priced or completed offering.
entries.controlImplication: Use the filing to test provider resilience assumptions against financing needs, compute commitments and reliance on a small group of strategic infrastructure partners.

entries.title: OpenAI describes expanded monitoring for frontier-model misalignment
entries.summary: On 29 October, OpenAI described a multilayer monitoring system covering a wider range of training, evaluation, internal-use and selected external-deployment settings, with human response for some high-priority alerts.
entries.whyItMatters: The company’s description follows independent historical testing of a prior pilot, but the new account is not an independent evaluation of current coverage or intervention effectiveness.
entries.controlImplication: Ask providers to specify which surfaces and workloads are monitored, what is excluded, expected alert and response times, and what independent testing supports the claims.
